name: Calcium thioglycolate depilatory

lead: Calcium thioglycolate is a salt of thioglycolic acid and the common active ingredient in over-the-counter depilatory creams. It lets people remove body and facial hair at the skin surface without a razor, leaving smooth skin that usually stays hair-free for several days.

It works chemically: the high-pH cream breaks the disulfide bonds in keratin so the hair softens and can be wiped away. Because it does not reach the follicle, hair regrows, as with shaving. A 1977 case series reported its use for excess hair caused by a blood-pressure drug.

paras: Products come as creams, gels, lotions, aerosols and roll-ons. The cream is spread over the hair for a few minutes, typically around 10 according to encyclopedic sources, then wiped or rinsed off. Users generally follow the label's timing and test a small patch first.

Thioglycolates are skin irritants in some clinical tests and can sensitize skin; they are also eye irritants. Case reports describe irritant dermatitis of the nails from a depilatory. Product labels advise against use on broken or sunburned skin and around the eyes.

Disulfide bonds in keratin break and hair softens
Hair wiped away, leaving smooth skin for days
angle.text: People use calcium thioglycolate creams to remove body or facial hair without shaving. Results last until regrowth, which encyclopedic sources place at several hours to several days.

lead: Calcium thioglycolate is the calcium salt of thioglycolic acid, and one of the main active ingredients of cream depilators sold over the counter. It is used to remove unwanted hair on legs, underarms, face and bikini line, giving the smooth look of a close shave without a blade.[1][2]

A depilatory cream commonly contains around 5 to 6 percent calcium thioglycolate in a cream base held near pH 12 with calcium or strontium hydroxide. It reduces the disulfide bonds of keratin, softening the hair shaft so that it can be wiped away after about 10 minutes.[1] Because the dermal papilla is not destroyed, hair grows back.[1]

Research is mostly toxicological and dermatological: a cosmetic ingredient safety assessment, in vitro eye-irritation tests that use calcium thioglycolate as a reference chemical, and case reports.[3][4][5] Brands including Nair, Veet and Magic Shave use thioglycolate chemistry.[1]
infobox: Cream, gel, lotion, aerosol, roll-on, powder

paras: Chemical depilatories are used on the legs, underarms, upper lip, and other body areas as an alternative to shaving, waxing or epilation. Because they cut hair at and just below the surface, regrowth is described as similar in timing to shaving rather than to root removal.[2][1]

A 1977 report described five women with hypertrichosis, a cosmetic side effect of the investigational antihypertensive minoxidil, who had the excess hair successfully removed with a calcium thioglycolate depilatory.[6] Chemical depilatories are also listed in reference texts as a option for hirsutism.[1] A 2026 case report describes topical calcium thioglycolate used for severe plantar hyperkeratosis in a patient with atopic dermatitis.[7]

Thioglycolates reduce cystine disulfide bonds in keratin, producing cysteine and dithiodiglycolic acid, and the alkaline cream hydrolyzes the weakened hair so it can be scraped off.[1][5] Hair-removal creams, gels, powders, aerosols and roll-ons all work in the same way according to a dermatology case report.[5]

A cosmetic ingredient safety review found thioglycolates penetrate skin and distribute to the kidneys, lungs, small intestine and spleen in animals, with excretion mostly in urine; they were slightly toxic orally in rats, were minimal to severe eye irritants, and could be skin irritants and sensitizers.[3] Clinical tests showed skin irritation in some cases, and the review reported no evidence of mutagenicity or carcinogenicity.[3]

A case report described irritant nail dermatitis with koilonychia after depilatory use.[5] In vitro eye-irritation validation studies use 5 percent calcium thioglycolate as a standard reference chemical.[8][9]
Depilatory ointments (psilothrum) were used in ancient Greece and Rome, and arsenic-and-lime pastes were later common. Sulfide-based products were replaced by thiols because of their odor.[1][2]

Calcium thioglycolate has also been studied in rats as an absorption enhancer for transdermal delivery and in environmental chemistry as a biochar modifier for heavy-metal removal; neither concerns appearance.[10][11]

Human studies are limited to a 1977 case series of five women treated for drug-induced hirsutism with a calcium thioglycolate depilatory,[6] a 2026 case report on plantar hyperkeratosis,[7] and a case report on nail irritation.[5] Clinical irritation data are summarized in the Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessment.[3]
